overview: Ayutthaya, founded on an island in the Chao Phraya in 1351, ruled Siam for four centuries and was one of the great trading cities of Asia. Its kings took the Khmer idea of divine kingship, and its port welcomed Chinese, Japanese, Persian, Dutch, Portuguese and French merchants.

items.text: Rice, deer hides, sappanwood and tin left through the royal warehouses; Chinese junks and, from 1511, Portuguese ships came to buy them.
Foreign quarters ringed the city: Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch from 1608, French and Persian; the Greek Constantine Phaulkon rose to chief minister under King Narai.
King Narai sent an embassy to Louis XIV at Versailles in 1686.
Prang towers in the Khmer manner and the tall chedis of Wat Phra Si Sanphet, with gilded Buddhas.
Court poetry, the Ramakien, the Thai Ramayana, and masked dance drama.
Theravada Buddhism with royal patronage and hundreds of temples in the capital.
Khmer court ritual and the devaraja idea of the king as a god shaped kingship; the law code of 1805 preserves Ayutthaya's laws.
The Historic City of Ayutthaya was listed by UNESCO.
Thai kingship, law and court culture descend from Ayutthaya.

fall.text: A Burmese army took and burned the city in April 1767. Within the year Taksin had rallied Siam from a new capital at Thonburi.
